text:
When you type "www.example.com" into your browser, you're initiating a process called DNS resolution. DNS, or Domain Name System, is like a phonebook for the internet. It translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses, which are the numerical addresses that computers use to communicate with each other.

Your browser needs to know the IP address of the server hosting the "www.example.com" website. Without this information, your browser wouldn't know where to send the request to fetch the webpage. The first step in DNS resolution is to find out which IP address corresponds to "www.example.com."

Your computer doesn't know the IP address of "www.example.com" off the top of its head, so it turns to a recursive resolver, which is like a local phonebook. The resolver starts by asking a root server, which is one of 13 global servers that manage the top-level domains. The root server doesn't know the exact IP address of "www.example.com," but it knows the IP address of the .com domain's authoritative name server. 

The resolver then asks the .com domain's authoritative name server, which knows the IP address of the "www.example.com" server. The authoritative name server sends back the IP address, and the resolver passes this information to your computer. If the resolver has this information in its cache, it can return the IP address immediately, saving time for future lookups.

However, if the resolver doesn't have the IP address in its cache, it will store the information for a certain period, defined by the Time to Live (TTL) value. This TTL value is like a timer that tells the resolver how long to keep the information before checking again. This caching mechanism speeds up future lookups for the same domain.

Once your computer has the IP address, it can send a request to the server at that IP address to fetch the webpage. DNS resolution is just the first step in the process of loading a webpage. After DNS resolution, your browser sends a request to the server, which then sends back the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files that make up the webpage. The browser then interprets these files and displays the webpage to you.
